subject: physics
topic: What is Ohm's law? Voltage, current and resistance, NCERT 12.3, V = I R, three cases, the V–I graph and the hot filament (60-second method, PD-26/27/28)

voice.note: stock English voice (PD-05); rate_scale 1.2 is the PD-28 fast-read plan (not yet measured; the quota is exhausted until 15 Nov 2026); re-measure on the first fast narration

outcome: The viewer can say what voltage, current and resistance are and their units (1 V = 1 J/C, 1 A = 1 C/s, 1 Ω = 1 V/A); state Ohm's law in plain words and recognise NCERT 12.3's statement with its condition; use V = I R, I = V/R and R = V/I on 2 V, 10 Ω → 0.20 A, 4 V → 0.40 A and 2 V, 20 Ω → 0.10 A; read the V–I graph as a straight line through the origin whose slope is R; and know that a hot filament bends the line.
claim_line: Twice the push, twice the flow.
cta_line: Try more cases in the free lesson.

artefacts.scroll_test: A meter showing '?' and one plain question, 'What is Ohm's law?', answered in a minute with three readings, NCERT's own sentence and a graph: a Class 10 student stays because they can feel the chapter fitting into one picture.
artefacts.surprise: Two numbers on the board decide the meter: double the push and the reading doubles, double the resistance and it halves, and a hot bulb bends the straight line.
artefacts.outcome: The viewer can say what voltage, current and resistance are and their units (1 V = 1 J/C, 1 A = 1 C/s, 1 Ω = 1 V/A); state Ohm's law in plain words and recognise NCERT 12.3's statement with its condition; use V = I R, I = V/R and R = V/I on 2 V, 10 Ω → 0.20 A, 4 V → 0.40 A and 2 V, 20 Ω → 0.10 A; read the V–I graph as a straight line through the origin whose slope is R; and know that a hot filament bends the line.
artefacts.prerequisite_boundary: Class 10: knows a cell, a wire and a bulb; has heard 'volt' and 'amp'; has not met Ohm's law. Coulomb and joule appear only on the unit cards.
artefacts.prerequisite_bridge: The meter counts charge per second (current); the resistor holds the flow back (resistance); the voltage across its ends is the push, energy per coulomb.

causal_chain: Voltage pushes, resistance holds back, the meter counts the current.
So I = V ÷ R: 2 V over 10 Ω gives 0.20 A.
Double V and I doubles; double R and I halves; V against I is a straight line of slope R.
All of that holds only while the temperature stays the same; a hot filament bends the line.

repair_log.original: Ohm's law: what's this meter reading? Let's calculate.
repair_log.replacement: What is Ohm's law? Something pushes electricity through a wire. That push is voltage, and we measure it in volts.
repair_log.reason: PD-27: clipped caption fragments read as AI-written; full sentences, plain word first, term second, unit third

repair_log.original: The resistor holds the flow back: resistance, ten ohms.
repair_log.replacement: Each wire holds the flow back a little; that is resistance, in ohms.
repair_log.reason: PD-27: no colon lists, no bare noun phrases

repair_log.original: In NCERT's words, the potential difference across a wire is directly proportional to the current through it, as long as its temperature stays the same. (draft, 26 words)
repair_log.replacement: Ohm's law says current grows in step with the push, while the temperature stays the same. (the verbatim NCERT sentence is on the card)
repair_log.reason: a 26-word sentence breaks the 18-word limit and the 60 s plan; the brief asks for the NCERT wording on the card and a simplified voice

repair_log.original: As a formula, voltage equals current times resistance, so current equals voltage divided by resistance. (draft)
repair_log.replacement: So V equals I R. Then I is V over R, and R is V over I.
repair_log.reason: adds the third rearrangement in fewer words; the letters are on the board chips from frame 0

repair_log.original: Here the battery pushes with two volts and the resistance is ten ohms, so the current is two divided by ten, which is point two amperes. (draft, 27 words)
repair_log.replacement: Two volts over ten ohms gives a current of point two amperes.
repair_log.reason: fit at 60 s; the board shows 2 V ÷ 10 Ω being built

repair_log.original: There is one catch. A hot wire, like the filament of a bulb, resists more, so the line bends. Ohm's law works only when the temperature stays the same. (draft)
repair_log.replacement: But a hot bulb filament resists more, so its line bends.
repair_log.reason: fit at 60 s; the condition is already spoken in b04, struck on the chip here and kept as point 3 of the answer sheet

scenes.title: One board: what Ohm's law is, three readings and its line

beats.text: What is Ohm's law? When electricity passes through a wire, something pushes it along. That push is called voltage, and we measure it in volts.
The flow is called current; this meter reads it in amperes.
